title: The body as temple
hookLine: Basavanna's poem and the Upanishad's line: the body is a shrine, so care is practice
carry: the body is a temple; someone holy lives here
last: YOUR EVENING ROUTINE — HAND THE WHOLE DAY BACK TO GOD.

cards: For two weeks you've been building a shrine: a shelf, a lamp, a flower, a bell, a cup of water. You've learned to keep it clean, bring fresh flowers, light it at the edges of the day. Now look down.
At your hands. Your feet. The chest going up and down.
There's a shrine you've carried this whole time, one you didn't have to buy, and it's easy to treat it worse than the shelf. Meals get skipped, sleep gets cut, and it only gets noticed when it hurts.
This week turns to the body and food. Today: the body as temple.

teach.h: THE BODY IS CALLED A TEMPLE.
teach.b: A short line in the Maitreya Upanishad says it straight out: the body is called a temple, and the living one inside it is Shiva himself. The body is the building. What lives in it is holy.
That's the teaching: the atman, the self within, is divine, so the body that houses it is a temple. You met atman on day ten: someone is in there. Today asks what that means for the building.
Basavanna, a poet-saint of Karnataka who wrote in Kannada, put it in a poem that's still sung. The rich, he says, build temples for Shiva. What can a poor man do?

teach.h: BASAVANNA: MY LEGS ARE THE PILLARS.
teach.b: Then he answers: my legs are the pillars, my body is the shrine, my head is the golden dome. He didn't need stone. He was already standing in one.
So looking after the body isn't vanity, and it isn't a chore separate from the spiritual life.

teach.h: CARE IS PART OF THE PRACTICE.
teach.b: Bathing before puja, eating with some care, sleeping enough, moving, resting: these become part of the practice, the way sweeping the shrine is part of puja. And notice what the idea doesn't say.

teach.h: A TEMPLE CAN BE OLD, OR CRACKED.
teach.b: The temple doesn't have to be perfect, young or strong. It can be old, cracked, patched, or hard to climb the steps of. Bodies that are sick, tired, disabled or aging are still temples, and still lived in.
The point is who lives there. This week is about caring for the building.

how: Many Hindus bathe before morning puja and treat bodily care, food, rest and movement as part of religious life, drawing on the idea, found in later Upanishads and in devotional poetry, that the body is a temple in which the divine dwells.

a market stall that sells flowers
a house of God: a temple

games.q: you're Basavanna, a poor man in a town where the rich are building grand stone temples for Shiva. what do you do?
o: save for years to build a small one.
say your own body is already the temple.
stop worshipping until you can afford it.
games.why: in his poem, his legs are the pillars, his body the shrine, his head the golden dome. he didn't need stone.

practice: Sit or lie down, whatever's kinder today, and close your eyes if you like.

Walk slowly through the temple: your feet, the foundation; the legs, Basavanna's pillars; the belly and chest, moving with the breath; the hands, which did so much work today; the shoulders, where the day usually hides; the face; the top of the head, the dome.
Don't fix anything, just visit each part. Someone holy lives here.

wordCard.voice: Devalaya, a house of God: the old idea that the body itself is this shrine, with someone holy living in it, so caring for it is part of the practice. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit devālaya: temple, literally a house of God. The Maitreya Upanishad calls the body one.

carryVoice: Your line: the body is a temple; someone holy lives here. A cracked temple is still lived in. See you tomorrow.
